questions.q: What is a mini-batch in the context of training a neural network?
options: The entire training dataset used for one gradient update
A single training example processed alone
A subset of the training data used to compute one gradient update
The validation set used after each epoch
questions.explain: Mini-batch gradient descent computes each update from a subset of the training data — a middle ground between single-example SGD and full-batch gradient descent.

questions.q: In `DataLoader(train_dataset, batch_size=32, shuffle=True, num_workers=2, pin_memory=True)`, what does `pin_memory=True` do?
options: Prevents the dataset from being shuffled
Speeds up CPU-to-GPU memory transfers when training on CUDA
Freezes the model's parameters during loading
Caches the entire dataset permanently in GPU memory
questions.explain: pin_memory=True places batches in page-locked host memory, which speeds up the transfer to a CUDA device.

questions.q: Why is a smaller batch size sometimes described as having a regularizing effect?
options: It increases the model's parameter count
It forces the use of dropout automatically
The noisier gradient estimate it produces can help training avoid sharp, poorly-generalizing minima
It disables weight decay
questions.explain: The extra gradient noise from estimating the gradient on a small subset of data can act like an implicit regularizer, nudging training away from sharp minima.

questions.q: What tradeoff typically comes with increasing batch size?
options: Gradient estimates get noisier and training slows down
Gradients become smoother and GPU utilization often improves, but activation memory usage rises
The model can no longer use backpropagation
The dataset must be re-labeled
questions.explain: Larger batches smooth the gradient estimate and typically push more work through the GPU per step, but activation memory scales roughly linearly with batch size.

questions.q: According to the linear scaling rule described in this lesson, if you increase batch size from 256 to 1024 (a 4x increase), what should you consider doing to the base learning rate?
options: Divide it by 4
Leave it exactly the same
Scale it up by roughly the same factor (about 4x), typically with a warmup period
Set it to zero
questions.explain: The linear scaling rule is a heuristic: scale the learning rate by roughly the same factor as the batch size increase, usually combined with a short warmup — then validate on real data.
